preamble: Total assimilation of the coda tap [ɾ] to a following [n], giving a geminate [nn]. In western Cuban Spanish (the provinces from Pinar del Río to Matanzas and Cienfuegos, including Havana, plus the municipalities of Corralillo and Trinidad), coda /ɾ/ and coda /l/ merge and assimilate to the next consonant; before /n/ both surface as [n], so pierna is pronounced pie[nn]a and carne [ˈkanːe]. The assimilation also applies across word boundaries. The unassimilated pronunciations remain more common. Arias (2019) assigns these realizations to the nasal phoneme /n/, because they are identical to those of /n/.

examples.note: Wikipedia (Caribbean Spanish) gives this as an example of assimilation causing gemination, "most notable of Spanish spoken in and around Havana".
Across a word boundary; Arias glosses the form as 'terminal novena o terminar novena', because coda /l/ gives the same result.
Arias contrasts ves naves, pronounced ve[hn]aves.
